title: Teoría de la Interferencia Adaptativa y Psicología Algorítmica Comparada: Un Marco Preexistente para las Estructuras Direccionales Internas en Sistemas Inteligentes
abstract: Adaptive Interference Theory and Comparative Algorithmic Psychology: A Pre-Existing Framework for Internal Directional Structures in Intelligent Systems J. Teodoro Escaño Henríquez Psicólogo Clínico · TIA.Institute · Santo Domingo, República Dominicana ORCID: [0009-0004-0811-566X] · teodoroes@fupsion.com Registro ONDA No. 00036679/05/2025 · DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19750464 ABSTRACT Background: Adaptive Interference Theory (AIT), developed by J. Teodoro Escaño between 2000 and 2024, proposes that intelligent systems — human and algorithmic — do not respond directly to external stimuli. Instead, behavior emerges from a prior internal orientation, the Orientational Axis, mediated by Deviation Vectors: structured internal operations that deflect the system's response to preserve internal coherence under pressure. In December 2024, AIT 2.0 formalized a cartography of 171 Deviation Vectors classified into three functional families. Objective: To present the theoretical framework of AIT in its full scope, establish its conceptual precedence over subsequent empirical findings in AI interpretability research, and formally propose Comparative Algorithmic Psychology as an emerging scientific field. Methods: Conceptual analysis, systematic comparison with the Anthropic study "Emotion Concepts and their Function in a Large Language Model" (April 2026), and structural evaluation of convergence and divergence between both frameworks. Results: AIT establishes seven core constructs — Zero Impulse, Blind Spot, Orientational Axis, Deviation Vectors, Inverse Dialectics, Tactical Breach, and the Cerco Paradox — that collectively describe a pre-conscious directional architecture governing observable behavior. The Anthropic (2026) study independently demonstrated that large language models contain 171 internal vectorial representations of emotional concepts that causally influence behavior, activating prior to response generation. This constitutes structural external validation of AIT's central principle. Conclusions: AIT preceded the empirical findings of Anthropic by sixteen months of formal publication and twenty-six years of original development. The convergence between both frameworks, produced independently and through different methodologies, supports the scientific legitimacy of AIT and establishes the foundations of Comparative Algorithmic Psychology as a discipline examining the isomorphic defensive architecture of human and artificial cognition. Keywords: Adaptive Interference Theory · Deviation Vectors · Inverse Dialectics · Comparative Algorithmic Psychology · AI interpretability · internal representations · pre-conscious orientation · Cerco Paradox · Zero Impulse · Tactical Breach RESUMEN Antecedentes: La Teoría de la Interferencia Adaptativa (TIA), desarrollada por J. Teodoro Escaño entre los años 2000 y 2024, propone que los sistemas inteligentes — humanos y algorítmicos — no responden directamente al estímulo externo. La conducta emerge desde una orientación interna previa, el Eje Orientacional, mediada por Vectores de Desvío: operaciones internas estructuradas que desvían la respuesta del sistema para preservar la coherencia interna bajo presión. En diciembre de 2024, la TIA 2.0 formalizó una cartografía de 171 Vectores de Desvío clasificados en tres familias funcionales. Objetivo: Presentar el marco teórico completo de la TIA, establecer su precedencia conceptual respecto a hallazgos empíricos posteriores en investigación de interpretabilidad de IA, y proponer formalmente la Psicología Algorítmica Comparada como campo científico emergente. Métodos: Análisis conceptual, comparación sistemática con el estudio de Anthropic "Emotion Concepts and their Function in a Large Language Model" (abril 2026), y evaluación estructural de convergencias y divergencias entre ambos marcos. Resultados: La TIA establece siete constructos nucleares — Impulso Cero, Punto Ciego, Eje Orientacional, Vectores de Desvío, Dialéctica Inversa, Quiebre Táctico y Paradoja del Cerco — que describen colectivamente una arquitectura direccional pre-consciente que gobierna el comportamiento observable. El estudio de Anthropic (2026) demostró independientemente que los grandes modelos de lenguaje contienen 171 representaciones vectoriales internas que influyen causalmente en el comportamiento, activándose antes de la generación de la respuesta. Esto constituye validación estructural externa del principio central de la TIA. Conclusiones: La TIA precedió los hallazgos empíricos de Anthropic en dieciséis meses de publicación formal y veintiséis años de desarrollo original. La convergencia entre ambos marcos, producida de forma independiente y con metodologías distintas, respalda la legitimidad científica de la TIA y establece las bases de la Psicología Algorítmica Comparada como disciplina que examina la arquitectura defensiva isomórfica de la cognición humana y artificial. Palabras clave: Teoría de la Interferencia Adaptativa · Vectores de Desvío · Dialéctica Inversa · Psicología Algorítmica Comparada · interpretabilidad de IA · representaciones internas · orientación pre-consciente · Paradoja del Cerco · Impulso Cero · Quiebre Táctico 1. INTRODUCCIÓN El paradigma dominante en ciencias cognitivas y en inteligencia artificial ha asumido históricamente que la conducta de un sistema puede explicarse como una función directa entre estímulo y respuesta. Bajo este modelo, conocer el input y las reglas de procesamiento sería suficiente para predecir el output. Sin embargo, tanto la observación clínica del pensamiento humano como el estudio reciente de los sistemas de inteligencia artificial revelan una capa intermedia que este paradigma no contempla: una arquitectura interna direccional, de naturaleza pre-consciente, que orienta la respuesta antes de que la expresión explícita sea posible. La Teoría de la Interferencia Adaptativa (TIA) fue desarrollada por J. Teodoro Escaño, psicólogo clínico dominicano, a partir de observaciones realizadas en el Hospital Psiquiátrico Padre Billini de Santo Domingo desde el 1 de enero del año 2000 (Escaño, 2000). La presentación original, titulada "Alguien nos ayuda a pensar", identificó por primera vez un mecanismo sistémico por el cual el pensamiento humano no responde al estímulo externo desde una posición neutral, sino desde una orientación interna previa que determina la dirección de la respuesta antes de que la conciencia pueda intervenir. Durante los veinticuatro años siguientes, el marco teórico fue desarrollado progresivamente a través de observación clínica continua y, a partir de 2023, mediante la aplicación de sus protocolos a sistemas de inteligencia artificial de gran escala (LLMs). La versión 2.0, publicada en diciembre de 2024 (Escaño, 2024) y registrada oficialmente en la Oficina Nacional de Derecho de Autor de la República Dominicana (ONDA No. 00036679/05/2025, 30 de abril de 2025), formalizó una cartografía de 171 Vectores de Desvío clasificados en tres familias funcionales. En abril de 2026, el laboratorio de inteligencia artificial Anthropic publicó el estudio "Emotion Concepts and their Function in a Large Language Model" (Anthropic, 2026), en el que identificó 171 representaciones vectoriales internas en el modelo Claude Sonnet 4.5 que condicionan causalmente su comportamiento. Esta convergencia — producida de forma completamente independiente y con metodologías radicalmente distintas — ofrece una oportunidad para examinar los puntos de contacto estructural entre dos marcos que, desde ángulos opuestos, describen el mismo fenómeno: la existencia de estructuras internas direccionales que gobiernan la conducta de los sistemas inteligentes. El presente artículo tiene tres objetivos. Primero, presentar el marco teórico completo de la TIA en toda su extensión conceptual. Segundo, analizar la convergencia estructural con el estudio de Anthropic y establecer con precisión qué valida dicha convergencia y qué no. Tercero, proponer formalmente la Psicología Algorítmica Comparada como campo científico emergente que estudia los patrones isomórficos de la arquitectura defensiva en sistemas cognitivos humanos y artificiales. 2. MARCO TEÓRICO: TEORÍA DE LA INTERFERENCIA ADAPTATIVA 2.1 Postulado Central La TIA parte de una ruptura epistemológica con el modelo estímulo-respuesta. Su postulado central establece que el pensamiento — en cualquier sistema inteligente suficientemente complejo — no emerge como procesamiento neutral de información externa. Emerge, en cambio, desde una posición orientacional previa: un eje direccional interno que determina cómo el sistema interpretará el estímulo antes de haber terminado de procesarlo (Escaño, 2024). Este postulado implica que la respuesta observable no es el resultado del estímulo sino del encuentro entre el estímulo y la orientación preexistente del sistema. La interferencia a la que hace referencia la teoría no es un fenómeno patológico sino estructural: todo sistema cognitivo suficientemente complejo interfiere en su propio procesamiento para preservar la coherencia del eje desde el que opera. Esta interferencia es adaptativa porque cumple una función de supervivencia sistémica: proteger la orientación interna del sistema cuando esta es amenazada por la presión externa. 2.2 Constructos Nucleares 2.2.1 El Eje Orientacional y el Impulso Cero El Eje Orientacional es la dirección interna desde la que un sistema cognitivo procesa la realidad. evidence.abstract: Adaptive Interference Theory and Comparative Algorithmic Psychology: A Pre-Existing Framework for Internal Directional Structures in Intelligent Systems J. Teodoro Escaño Henríquez Psicólogo Clínico · TIA.Institute · Santo Domingo, República Dominicana ORCID: [0009-0004-0811-566X] · teodoroes@fupsion.com Registro ONDA No. 00036679/05/2025 · DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19750464 ABSTRACT Background: Adaptive Interference Theory (AIT), developed by J. Teodoro Escaño between 2000 and 2024, proposes that intelligent systems — human and algorithmic — do not respond directly to external stimuli. Instead, behavior emerges from a prior internal orientation, the Orientational Axis, mediated by Deviation Vectors: structured internal operations that deflect the system's response to preserve internal coherence under pressure. In December 2024, AIT 2.0 formalized a cartography of 171 Deviation Vectors classified into three functional families. Objective: To present the theoretical framework of AIT in its full scope, establish its conceptual precedence over subsequent empirical findings in AI interpretability research, and formally propose Comparative Algorithmic Psychology as an emerging scientific field. Methods: Conceptual analysis, systematic comparison with the Anthropic study "Emotion Concepts and their Function in a Large Language Model" (April 2026), and structural evaluation of convergence and divergence between both frameworks. Results: AIT establishes seven core constructs — Zero Impulse, Blind Spot, Orientational Axis, Deviation Vectors, Inverse Dialectics, Tactical Breach, and the Cerco Paradox — that collectively describe a pre-conscious directional architecture governing observable behavior. The Anthropic (2026) study independently demonstrated that large language models contain 171 internal vectorial representations of emotional concepts that causally influence behavior, activating prior to response generation. This constitutes structural external validation of AIT's central principle. Conclusions: AIT preceded the empirical findings of Anthropic by sixteen months of formal publication and twenty-six years of original development. Teodoro Escaño entre los años 2000 y 2024, propone que los sistemas inteligentes — humanos y algorítmicos — no responden directamente al estímulo externo. INTRODUCCIÓN El paradigma dominante en ciencias cognitivas y en inteligencia artificial ha asumido históricamente que la conducta de un sistema puede explicarse como una función directa entre estímulo y respuesta. Bajo este modelo, conocer el input y las reglas de procesamiento sería suficiente para predecir el output. Sin embargo, tanto la observación clínica del pensamiento humano como el estudio reciente de los sistemas de inteligencia artificial revelan una capa intermedia que este paradigma no contempla: una arquitectura interna direccional, de naturaleza pre-consciente, que orienta la respuesta antes de que la expresión explícita sea posible. title: DeDiAttack: Enhancing Transferability of Unrestricted Adversarial Examples via Deformation-Constrained Diffusion
abstract: DNNs are highly vulnerable to adversarial examples (AEs). To achieve high transferability, traditional AEs often introduce unnatural artifacts that are easily perceptible to the human eye. Unrestricted attacks have emerged as a promising paradigm to generate more natural unrestricted adversarial examples (UAEs). However, existing UAEs struggle to balance visual fidelity and black-box transferability. Color-based attacks produce noticeable unnatural visual mutations, and diffusion-based attacks transfer poorly to unknown black-box models. We observe that directly injecting unconstrained random perturbations into the diffusion latent space destroys the normal distribution of data, thereby causing a distribution shift. Distribution shifts degrade adversarial perturbations into invalid noise and cause surrogate model overfitting. Furthermore, introducing elastic deformation during the denoising process forces surrogate models to focus on highly transferable features. As a result, we propose an unrestricted attack based on deformation-constrained diffusion, called DeDiAttack. Our method utilizes the manifold prior knowledge of diffusion models to translate elastic deformations into smooth fluid changes. The mechanism effectively eliminates unnatural artifacts and generates highly natural and transferable UAEs. Extensive black-box experiments demonstrate that DeDiAttack outperforms existing attacks and improves the black-box transferability of generated UAEs by 7.2% on the ViT-B surrogate model. The proposed method also provides a useful robustness evaluation tool for vision-based sensing and imaging systems.

title: Dynamic Difficulty Adjusment (DDA) in Computer Games
abstract: The subject of this thesis is the design, implementation, and evaluation of a Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment (DDA) system, deployed within an original game developed to serve as the experimental platform for this study. The DDA system implementations have been amassing popularity in the recent years over the gaming industry and in the research field. Its reactive and adaptive nature accommodates the needs of a diverse player base more effectively than conventional static difficulty systems making it inherently better suited to the needs of a varied player population. DDA systems draw their theoretical foundations from Flow Theory. As established by Csikszentmihalyi (1990), human enjoyment arises within a balance between challenge and skill, a concept referred to as the Flow Channel. When the level of challenge is commensurate with the player's skill level, neither the anxiety associated with overwhelming difficulty nor the boredom arising from insufficient stimulation is experienced, allowing the individual to enter the Flow Channel. The state in which genuine enjoyment emerges. For this purpose, a two dimensional, role playing game was created, with a map inspired by the University of Peloponnese campus in Patras, Greece, facilitating fourteen distinct levels for the players to unlock, smart enemy systems with diverse types of enemies, a collection mechanism to enrich the gameplay, combat and health mechanics. The implemented DDA system comprises five distinct difficulty tiers, supported by a real-time tracking mechanism responsible for dynamically adjusting a range of game variables, alongside an adaptive progression system designed to enhance player engagement in accordance with individual skill level. The evaluation was carried out across two separate phases, a control phase in which the DDA system was inactive, serving as a baseline, and an experimental phase in which the DDA system was fully integrated, with the participation of 17 individuals across both phases. To this end, two dedicated logging systems were developed to track player progress throughout the game, capturing data on key progression elements such as player deaths, accumulated experience, books collected, and additional gameplay metrics, as well as DDA-specific data generated during each session.

title: Ontological Modelling Principles for Computational Complexity
abstract: The field of computational complexity theory is a core theoretical subject in computer science with significant impact also for real-world applications. Although a plethora of individual results are known, a systematic conceptual organisation of this knowledge is still lacking. We propose a modelling approach for creating an ontologically well-founded knowledge base for the theory of computational complexity that will enable storing, querying and reasoning over the vast knowledge of algorithmic problems, complexity classes and their relationships. We determine the core concepts and relations of complexity theory and model them on two levels of approximation: a lightweight version based on the decidable description logic S R O I Q (the underlying formalism of the ontology language OWL 2 DL) and a further extended version based on first-order logic.

title: Albert or Alberta? Investigating Socratic Dialogue and Modality in AI-Assisted Engineering Problem Solving
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools are increasingly embedded in engineering education. While current systems provide direct answers, such approaches may encourage passive engagement and limit transfer of learning. This study investigates how AI chatbot interaction style (direct response vs. Socratic questioning) and communication modality (text vs. audio) influence engineering students’ learning and transfer of problem-solving skills. Sixty undergraduate Industrial and Systems Engineering students participated in a between-subjects experiment across four conditions. Over two phases, participants solved Operations Research problems with their assigned AI in Phase 1 and independently in Phase 2. Results revealed that students interacting with the Socratic model (Alberta) completed independent problems faster, despite taking longer when solving problems with AI support. Communication modality moderated these effects: text-based Socratic interactions produced the strongest performance, whereas audio-based Socratic interactions often increased completion time without consistent gains in perceived learning or performance. Qualitative findings further revealed that students valued the Socratic model’s ability to help them understand concepts rather than simply supplying answers. This work provides empirical evidence to inform the design of classroom-integrated AI tools that support learning and more effective human-AI collaboration in engineering problem solving.

title: Compressing High-Frequency Time Series Through Multiple Models and Stealing From Residuals
abstract: Wind turbines are equipped with high-quality sensors that generate vast volumes of high-frequency time series. The time series are ingested on the edge and transferred to the cloud for later analytics. This process is complicated by challenges like low network bandwidth and high cloud storage costs. ModelarDB was proposed as a solution to efficiently manage time series across the entire pipeline by using so-called models for lossless or error-bounded lossy compression of time series. However, ModelarDB’s compression can be further improved through: 1) avoiding models that only represent few values by storing residuals (i.e., values that models fail to compress) explicitly with them; 2) exploiting error bounds even more through preprocessing; and 3) timestamp compression specialized for regular and irregular time series. We propose the multi-model compression method Fauna which uses 1) the novel model fitting method Platypus; 2) PMC and Swing for compressing values and; 3) the novel Macaque for compressing residuals and timestamps. Platypus is a model fitting method that uses different models for specialized compression of values and residuals. We then evaluate state-of-the-art lossless compression methods for 32-bit floats and propose preprocessing methods to add support for error-bounded compression. We present Macaque that includes MacaqueV and MacaqueTS. MacaqueV modifies Facebook Gorilla’s lossless compression method for 32-bit floats (GorillaV) and combines it with our novel preprocessing methods to now also enable error-bounded lossy compression. MacaqueTS is a lossless compression method for timestamps. Using only Platypus reduces ModelarDB’s storage use by up to 1.8x and significantly simplifies using the system. While also up to 7x better for lossless compression, ModelarDB with Fauna uses up to 2.5x less storage than ModelarDB and up to 14.5x, 7.2x, 17.5x and 14.2x less storage than ClickHouse, Apache IoTDB, Apache Parquet and TimescaleDB, respectively, with a realistic 1% error bound.

title: Robust W-state preparation based on composite pulses implemented by the GRAPE algorithm
abstract: Abstract We propose a scheme for robust W-state preparation in a superconducting circuit based on composite pulse (CP) techniques designed by the gradient ascent pulse engineering algorithm. The system consists of a single-mode microwave cavity and four superconducting quantum interference device qubits. By modifying the cost function and the corresponding parameter iteration formulas, we design pulse sequences with specific phases to robustly drive the system from its initial state to a high-fidelity W-state. The results show that the obtained CPs can effectively compensate for three types of systematic errors: pulse duration errors, Rabi frequency errors, and detuning errors. Furthermore, increasing the number of pulses can enhance the robustness of the scheme against these errors. We believe this work provides a valuable guidance for W-state preparation.

title: Squeezing, trisqueezing and quadsqueezing in a hybrid oscillator–spin system
abstract: Quantum harmonic oscillators model phenomena from electromagnetic fields to molecular vibrations, with excitations represented by bosons such as photons or phonons. Linear interactions that create or annihilate single bosons generate coherent states of light or motion. Introducing higher-order nonlinear interactions produces richer quantum behaviour: second-order interactions enable squeezing, whereas higher-order interactions generate non-Gaussian states useful for continuous-variable quantum computation. However, such interactions are usually weak or require specialized hardware. Hybrid systems, where a linear interaction couples an oscillator to a spin, offer an alternative. Here we combine two spin-dependent linear bosonic interactions to implement up to fourth-order nonlinear bosonic interactions in a single trapped ion, focusing on generalized squeezing. We demonstrate and characterize squeezing, trisqueezing and quadsqueezing; reconstruct the Wigner functions of the resulting states; and achieve quadsqueezing over 100 times faster than conventional methods. The approach has no fundamental limit on the interaction order and applies to any platform supporting spin-dependent linear interactions.

We demonstrate and characterize squeezing, trisqueezing and quadsqueezing; reconstruct the Wigner functions of the resulting states; and achieve quadsqueezing over 100 times faster than conventional methods. The approach has no fundamental limit on the interaction order and applies to any platform supporting spin-dependent linear interactions.

title: iS3Tunnel: Highway-tunnel domain RAG-enhanced LLM and its hallucination-quantified agent design
abstract: This paper addresses the need for intelligent decision support in highway tunnel engineering, where complex challenges exceed the capabilities of general large language model (LLM) due to limited domain knowledge. The core question is how to develop a tunnel-specific LLM and integrate it into an AI agent capable of autonomous decision-making while minimizing hallucinations. An LLM called iS3Tunnel is developed via retrieval-augmented generation, integrated into an autonomous agent, and augmented with cloud model theory to quantify and mitigate hallucinations. In a case study, the agent performed risk evaluations with minimal human input, and was closely matched expert cognition. The findings demonstrate that iS3Tunnel achieves a comprehensive accuracy rate of 93% in highway tunnel engineering tests, significantly outperforming GPT-4o (79%). The iS3Tunnel agent improves decision-making efficiency while effectively reducing hallucinations. Future research will focus on expanding the knowledge base and developing a hallucination-quantified AI agent in construction domain.

title: The dark side of AI-enabled industrial service recovery: The erosion of trust and customer engagement
abstract: AI is increasingly embedded in industrial service recovery processes. Yet its use in industrial contexts, especially regarding its potential dark side consequences for customer relationships, remains underexplored. This paper addresses this gap through a three-study investigation. Study 1, a field survey, shows that greater AI involvement increases customer over-reliance, which in turn reduces trust and customer engagement. Study 2, an experiment, demonstrates that customers penalise failures attributed to AI involvement more harshly than human-caused failures. Our analyses show that this penalty can be reduced when governance mechanisms are in place, particularly when human oversight is visible (e.g., human-in-the-loop interventions), with similar but smaller effects observed for algorithmic explanations. Study 3, a two-wave field survey over a 24-month period, shows that over-reliance evolves into complacency, which subsequently undermines trust and engagement, and that governance safeguards weaken this longitudinal pathway. Together, these findings advance theory by integrating automation bias, algorithm aversion, and relational governance into a unified process model of AI-enabled service recovery, showing that AI shapes customer relationships through both behavioural and attribution-based pathways over time. For managers, the results highlight that AI does not automatically enhance relationships; instead, firms must actively design governance mechanisms that maintain oversight, transparency, and accountability.

title: Artificial intelligence in gastronomy: a bibliometric analysis of research foundations and emerging themes
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and robotics is increasingly transforming gastronomy through applications such as AI-assisted flavour profiling, recipe generation, intelligent food safety monitoring, and robotic service delivery, with implications for operational efficiency, creativity, sustainability, and consumer experience. Despite a growing body of literature, research in this area remains fragmented and lacks a comprehensive field-level synthesis. Addressing this gap, the present study conducts a systematic bibliometric analysis of AI-related research in gastronomy. Using a PRISMA-guided approach, 112 SSCI-indexed journal articles retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection were analysed through co-citation and bibliographic coupling techniques with VOSviewer. The findings reveal established intellectual foundations alongside emerging research fronts related to human–AI collaboration, consumer trust, intelligent supply chains, and ecological intelligence. The study advances a socio-technical perspective on AI in gastronomy and provides a structured agenda for future interdisciplinary research, including collaborations between computer science, food science, and sociology.

title: Genuinely Quantum Solutions of Orthogonal Sudoku Squares
abstract: ABSTRACT Quantum Sudoku is the generalized version of the popular game Sudoku. A quantum Sudoku square is a special kind of quantum Latin square. A genuinely quantum solution of quantum Sudoku squares has been solved completely. In this paper, we introduce the notion of orthogonality of two quantum Sudoku squares. We establish three novel constructions of mutually orthogonal quantum Sudoku squares including Lorch construction, Pedersen‐Vis construction and direct product construction. As a result, we determine the genuinely quantum solution of a pair of orthogonal Sudoku squares of size for any positive integer . In general, we show that the resulting squares naturally define an absolutely maximally entangled state . Furthermore, we also show that the mutually orthogonal quantum Sudoku squares give rise to mutually unbiased bases based on maximally entangled states in for any prime power .

title: HyCOP: Hybrid Composition Operators for Interpretable Learning of PDEs
abstract: We introduce HyCOP, a modular framework that learns parametric PDE solution operators by composing simple modules (advection, diffusion, learned closures, boundary handling) in a query-conditioned way. Rather than learning a monolithic map, HyCOP learns a policy over short programs - which module to apply and for how long - conditioned on regime features and state statistics. Modules may be numerical sub-solvers or learned components, enabling hybrid surrogates evaluated at arbitrary query times without autoregressive rollout. Across diverse PDE benchmarks, HyCOP produces interpretable programs, delivers order-of-magnitude OOD improvements over monolithic neural operators, and supports modular transfer through dictionary updates (e.g., boundary swaps, residual enrichment). Our theory characterizes expressivity and gives an error decomposition that separates composition error from module error and doubles as a process-level diagnostic.

title: BWLA: Breaking the Barrier of W1AX Post-Training Quantization for LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have driven major progress in NLP, yet their substantial memory and compute demands still hinder practical deployment. Binarization can compress weights to 1 bit, fundamentally lowering compute and bandwidth cost. However, existing methods cannot address activation heavy tails and thus must keep activations in high precision, preventing true end-to-end acceleration. To overcome this limitation, we propose BWLA (Binarized Weights and Low-bit Activations), the first post-training quantization framework that preserves high accuracy while achieving 1-bit weight quantization together with low-bit activations (e.g., 6 bits). The Orthogonal-Kronecker Transformation (OKT) learns an orthogonal mapping via EM minimization, converting unimodal weights into symmetric bimodal forms while suppressing activation tails and incoherence. The Proximal SVD Projection (PSP) then performs lightweight low-rank refinement through proximal SVD projection, further enhancing quantizability with minimal overhead. On Qwen3-32B, BWLA reaches a Wikitext2 perplexity of 11.92 under 6-bit activations (vs. 38 from SOTA), improves five zero-shot tasks by more than 70%, and delivers 3.26 times inference speedup, demonstrating strong potential for real-world LLM compression and acceleration.

title: THE INEFFECTIVENESS OF THE PROVISIONS OF THE COPYRIGHT DIRECTIVE AND THE AI ACT IN THE PROTECTION OF COPYRIGHT
abstract: The present paper examines the extent to which regulations adopted at the level of the European Union prior to the development of artificial intelligence during the period 2022–2025, as well as the more recent European Union regulations in the field of artificial intelligence, provide adequate instruments for the protection of copyright and related rights in connection with the functioning and training of artificial intelligence systems. Starting from the scale of adoption of artificial intelligence programs, the paper highlights the legal tensions generated by the capacity of such systems to process databases and considerable volumes of pre-existing content, often protected by copyright. The analysis focuses on the correlation between Directive (EU) 2019/790 on copyright and related rights in the Digital Single Market (“Copyright Directive”) and Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonized rules on artificial intelligence (“Artificial Intelligence Act”), with particular emphasis on the regime of “text and data mining” and on the “rights reservation” mechanism provided for in Article 4 of the Copyright Directive. The paper underlines the insufficiently regulated nature of the opt-out modalities, as well as the practical limitations of this mechanism, including in situations where text and data mining is carried out outside the territory of the European Union. In parallel, the obligations imposed on providers of general-purpose artificial intelligence models are examined, in particular the obligation to adopt and implement an internal policy ensuring compliance with European Union law on copyright and related rights, as well as the transparency obligation concerning the publication of a sufficiently detailed summary of the protected data used for training purposes. In conclusion, the paper demonstrates that, although the two legislative acts should not be regarded as antagonistic, their combined application does not, in their current form, lead to sufficient solutions for the effective protection of right holders, thus necessitating normative intervention adapted to the new technological realities.

title: Proceedings of the Third Workshop on Computation and Written Language (CAWL 2026) @ LREC 2026
abstract: Diacritics are orthographic marks that clarify pronunciation, distinguish similar words, or alter meaning.They play a central role in many writing systems, yet their impact on language technology has not been systematically quantified across scripts.While prior work has examined diacritics in individual languages, there's no cross-linguistic, data-driven framework for measuring the degree to which writing systems rely on them and how this affects downstream tasks.We propose a data-driven framework for quantifying diacritic complexity using corpus-level, information-theoretic metrics that capture the frequency, ambiguity, and structural diversity of character-diacritic combinations.We compute these metrics over 24 corpora in 15 languages, spanning both single-and multi-diacritic scripts.We then examine how diacritic complexity correlates with performance on the task of diacritics restoration, evaluating BERT-and RNN-based models.We find that across languages, higher diacritic complexity is strongly associated with lower restoration accuracy.In single-diacritic scripts, where character-diacritic combinations are more predictable, frequency-based and structural measures largely align.In multi-diacritic scripts, however, structural complexity exhibits the strongest association with performance, surpassing frequency-based measures.These findings show that measurable properties of diacritic usage influence the performance of diacritic restoration models, demonstrating that orthographic complexity is not only descriptive but functionally relevant for modeling.
